1:2.t: Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor. Paul founded churches in its southern part on his first journey (Acts 13-14).

1:17.t: Arabia: the Nabatean kingdom east and south of Damascus.

1:18.t: "To get acquainted with": the KJV's "to see"; Greek historesai, to visit in order to learn from.

1:19.t: James, the brother of the Lord, who became the leader of the Jerusalem church; see Acts 12:17.

2:1.t: This visit may be the one of Acts 11:30, or the Jerusalem council of Acts 15.

2:9.t: "Cephas": Peter. "Pillars": leaders, like the pillars that hold up a building.

2:12.t: "The circumcision group": Jewish believers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised.

2:14.t: It is not clear where Paul's words to Peter end and his comment to the Galatians begins; the quotation marks follow one common reading.

3:13.t: "Redeemed" (Greek exagorazo): bought out, as a slave is bought out of the market. "Becoming a curse for us": Christ took the curse in our place.

3:16.t: A quotation of Genesis 12:7, 13:15 and 24:7. "Seed" (Hebrew zera, Greek sperma) is a collective noun; Paul draws attention to the singular to point to Christ.

4:10.t: Days, months, seasons and years: probably the Jewish Sabbaths, new moons, festivals and sabbatical years, which the false teachers required.

4:13.t: "In the weakness of the flesh": the KJV's "through infirmity of the flesh", probably an illness. Compare 4:15 and 2 Corinthians 12:7.

4:24.t: Hagar was Abraham's slave and the mother of Ishmael (Genesis 16, 21).
"Taken figuratively" (Greek allegoroumena): the KJV's "an allegory". Paul reads the story of Hagar and Sarah as a picture of two covenants.

5:12.t: Pagan priests of the goddess Cybele, well known in Galatia, castrated themselves.

5:19.t: "Adultery": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have this word in verse 19. "Murders": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have this word in verse 21.

6:11.t: "How large a letter": the KJV's reading. The Greek can also mean "with what large letters", Paul's own large handwriting at the end of a dictated letter.

6:15.t: "In Christ Jesus": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

1:6.t: "A different gospel" (Greek heteron euangelion): the false teachers added circumcision and keeping the law of Moses as conditions for Gentiles to belong to God's people. "Under God's curse" (Greek anathema): devoted to destruction, cursed; see 1 Corinthians 16:22.

2:16.t: "Faith in Jesus Christ" (Greek pistis Iesou Christou): The Greek can mean faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ; both are true in Paul, and this translation follows the more traditional reading (see Romans 3:22). "Works of the law": the deeds the law of Moses requires; readers disagree on whether Paul means the law as a whole as a way of earning right standing, or especially the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath (see Romans 3:20). "Justified": declared righteous, acquitted, put right with God (see Romans 3:24).

2:20.t: "I have been crucified with Christ": by faith the believer shares in Christ's death and new life (Romans 6:3-8). "Loved me and gave Himself for me": Paul makes Christ's love personal.

3:24.t: "Guardian" (Greek paidagogos): the KJV's "schoolmaster". A paidagogos was not a teacher but a household slave who supervised a child and took him to school. The law guarded God's people until Christ came.

3:27.t: "Clothed yourselves with Christ" (Greek Christon enedysasthe): the KJV's "put on Christ", like putting on a garment that marks one's new identity.

3:28.t: "All one in Christ Jesus": the divisions of nation, social status and sex no longer determine standing before God or belonging to His people. Paul does not deny that the differences exist.

4:3.t: "Elemental spiritual forces" (Greek stoicheia): the KJV's "elements". The word can mean basic principles (the ABCs), the physical elements, or spiritual powers thought to rule the world. Paul puts life under the law and pagan religion in the same category of slavery.

4:9.t: "Elemental spiritual forces" (Greek stoicheia): the KJV's "elements". The word can mean basic principles (the ABCs), the physical elements, or spiritual powers thought to rule the world. Paul puts life under the law and pagan religion in the same category of slavery.

4:4.t: "When the set time had fully come" (Greek to pleroma tou chronou): the KJV's "the fulness of the time", the right moment in God's plan.

4:5.t: "Adoption to sonship" (Greek huiothesia): a Roman adopted son received full legal rights as heir; see Romans 8:15. "Abba": Aramaic for "Father", the word a child used for his father, warm and respectful; see Mark 14:36.

5:4.t: "Fallen away from grace" (Greek tes charitos exepesate): to seek justification by the law is to leave the sphere of grace altogether.

5:6.t: "Faith expressing itself through love" (Greek pistis di agapes energoumene): faith that works through love. True faith is never idle.

5:16.t: "Flesh ... Spirit": "flesh" here means human nature apart from God, weak and ruled by sin, not the physical body as such; the Spirit is God's own Spirit living in believers. See Romans 7:14 and 8:4-9.

5:22.t: "Fruit" (Greek karpos): singular. One fruit, with nine qualities, grown by the Spirit, unlike the many "works" of the flesh. "Forbearance" (Greek makrothymia): the KJV's "longsuffering", patience. "Faithfulness" (Greek pistis): the KJV's "faith", here meaning reliability. "Gentleness" (Greek prautes): the KJV's "meekness", not weakness but gentle, humble strength; see Matthew 5:5. "Self-control" (Greek enkrateia): the KJV's "temperance", mastery over one's desires; see Acts 24:25.

6:2.t: "Burdens ... load" (Greek bare ... phortion): two different words. Bare are heavy burdens others help to carry; phortion is a soldier's pack, one's own responsibility.

6:5.t: "Burdens ... load" (Greek bare ... phortion): two different words. Bare are heavy burdens others help to carry; phortion is a soldier's pack, one's own responsibility.

6:16.t: "The Israel of God": readers understand this as the church, Jew and Gentile together, as Jewish believers, or as the faithful of Israel who will come to believe.

6:17.t: "Marks" (Greek stigmata): brands, like those marking a slave as his master's property. Paul's scars from beatings mark him as Christ's.
